lesson.title: The Bridge Reaction: Pyruvate's One-Way Trip Into the Mitochondrion
lesson.summary: Pyruvate oxidation is the irreversible bridge step that converts each pyruvate from glycolysis into acetyl-CoA, releasing CO2 and generating NADH before the carbon skeleton ever enters the Krebs cycle.
lesson.body:
Glycolysis ends with two pyruvate molecules sitting in the cytoplasm, but they cannot enter the Krebs cycle as they are. Pyruvate first has to be transported across both membranes of the mitochondrion into the mitochondrial matrix, and then chemically converted through a step often called the bridge reaction or pyruvate oxidation. This step happens twice per glucose molecule, once for each pyruvate, and it is worth remembering that doubling whenever you compare its output to the single-molecule Krebs cycle reactions you will study next.

The reaction itself is catalyzed by a large, multi-enzyme assembly called the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, and it does three things at once. It removes a carboxyl group from pyruvate and releases it as carbon dioxide, a decarboxylation. It oxidizes the remaining two-carbon fragment, transferring electrons to NAD+ and reducing it to NADH, the same redox chemistry you saw drive glycolysis's own NADH production. And it attaches that two-carbon fragment to coenzyme A, forming the high-energy thioester bond that defines acetyl-CoA, the product examined in detail in the next section. Written simply: pyruvate plus NAD+ plus coenzyme A yields acetyl-CoA plus NADH plus CO2.

The pyruvate dehydrogenase complex needs an unusually large toolkit of cofactors to accomplish this, including thiamine pyrophosphate, derived from vitamin B1, lipoic acid, FAD, NAD+, and coenzyme A itself, derived from vitamin B5. That dependence on multiple vitamin-derived cofactors is a good reminder of why B-vitamin deficiencies can directly impair cellular energy metabolism.

A crucial detail students often miss is that pyruvate oxidation is effectively irreversible under normal cellular conditions. Once a carbon atom leaves as CO2 here, that specific carbon can never be reassembled back into glucose through the reverse of this reaction, which is one reason the human body cannot convert fats, whose breakdown also funnels through acetyl-CoA, back into net new glucose. The reaction's irreversibility also makes it a natural regulatory checkpoint: the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is inhibited when NADH and ATP are already abundant, preventing the cell from producing more acetyl-CoA than the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain can actually use.

Tallying the output across one full glucose molecule, pyruvate oxidation happening twice yields 2 NADH, 2 CO2, and 2 acetyl-CoA molecules, in addition to the 2 ATP and 2 NADH already produced by glycolysis. Those 2 NADH from this step alone will later feed directly into the electron transport chain from inside the mitochondrial matrix, unlike the 2 NADH from glycolysis, which are made in the cytoplasm and must be shuttled in by a separate mechanism discussed when we calculate total ATP yield.

It is also worth noting how small this step looks on paper compared to how essential it is. Only one CO2 and one NADH come from each pyruvate here, far less than the Krebs cycle will extract from the resulting acetyl-CoA, yet without this single bridging reaction none of the two-carbon fuel produced by glycolysis could ever reach the Krebs cycle machinery waiting inside the mitochondrial matrix.
